agent.system_template:
You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

Shellharden
===========

Shellharden is a tool that highlights shell scripts and can semi-automatically
apply safe quoting changes to help scripts conform to common shell safety
recommendations (such as those suggested by ShellCheck).

Usage
-----

Basic usage:

    shellharden [OPTIONS] [FILE]

- Without options, shellharden reads the provided FILE (or stdin) and prints
  a syntax-highlighted version to stdout.
- Use the --transform option to apply suggested quoting/rewrites to the input.
  Do not use --transform blindly: review the proposed changes before applying,
  as some scripts may intentionally rely on behavior that the tool would
  change.

Examples
--------

- View a highlighted script on the terminal:

    shellharden example.sh

- Show suggested transformations (preview mode):

    shellharden --preview example.sh

- Apply suggested changes (review first):

    shellharden --transform -o example.fixed.sh example.sh

Safety advice
-------------

Automatic transformations may alter the semantics of a script. Always review
changes created with --transform and consult the accompanying guidance on safe
shell scripting if you are unsure.

For more information about safe shell practices, see how_to_do_things_safely_in_bash.md (if present).

LICENSE
-------

This repository contains license files that govern usage of the project. See the
LICENSE file for details.

Shellharden: The corrective bash syntax highlighter.

Usage:
	shellharden [options] [files]
	cat files | shellharden [options] ''

Shellharden is a syntax highlighter and a tool to semi-automate the rewriting
of scripts to ShellCheck conformance, mainly focused on quoting.

The default mode of operation is like `cat`, but with syntax highlighting in
foreground colors and suggestive changes in background colors.

Options:
	--suggest         Output a colored diff suggesting changes.
	--syntax          Output syntax highlighting with ANSI colors.
	--syntax-suggest  Diff with syntax highlighting (default mode).
	--transform       Output suggested changes.
	--check           No output; exit with 2 if changes are suggested.
	--replace         Replace file contents with suggested changes.
	--                Don't treat further arguments as options.
	-h|--help         Show help text.
	--version         Show version.

The changes suggested by Shellharden inhibits word splitting and indirect
pathname expansion. This will make your script ShellCheck compliant in terms of
quoting. Whether your script will work afterwards is a different question:
If your script was using those features on purpose, it obviously won't anymore!

Every script is possible to write without using word splitting or indirect
pathname expansion, but it may involve doing things differently.
See the accompanying file how_to_do_things_safely_in_bash.md or online:
https://github.com/anordal/shellharden/blob/master/how_to_do_things_safely_in_bash.md

{"command":"python3 -c '
import subprocess

my_bin = "./target/release/shellharden"
orig_bin = "./executable"

modes = ["--syntax", "--suggest", "--syntax-suggest", "--transform", "--check"]

test_cases = [
    "echo $foo",
    "echo ${foo}",
    "echo \"$foo\"",
    "echo \"${foo}\"",
    "echo $foo $bar",
    "echo $foo/bar",
    "echo $foo_bar",
    "echo ${foo}_bar",
    "echo $1",
    "echo $@",
    "echo $*",
    "echo $#",
    "echo $?",
    "echo $$",
    "echo $!",
    "echo ${#foo}",
    "echo $(cmd)",
    "echo `cmd`",
    "echo \"`cmd`\"",
    "echo $((1+1))",
    "foo=$bar",
    "export foo=$bar",
    "echo $10",
    "echo \"unclosed",
]

total = 0
passed = 0

for tc in test_cases:
    for mode in modes:
        total += 1
        res1 = subprocess.run([orig_bin, mode, ""], input=tc + "\n", text=True, capture_output=True)
        res2 = subprocess.run([my_bin, mode, ""], input=tc + "\n", text=True, capture_output=True)

        ok = (res1.returncode == res2.returncode and res1.stdout == res2.stdout and res1.stderr == res2.stderr)
        if ok:
            passed += 1
        else:
            print(f"FAILED for input={tc!r}, mode={mode}")
            print(f"  ORIG exit={res1.returncode}, out={res1.stdout!r}, err={res1.stderr!r}")
            print(f"  MINE exit={res2.returncode}, out={res2.stdout!r}, err={res2.stderr!r}")

print(f"PASSED {passed} / {total}")
'"}

import subprocess
import os

my_bin = "./target/release/shellharden"
orig_bin = "./executable"

# 1. Complex scripts
complex_scripts = [
    """#!/bin/bash
# Test script
function test_func() {
    local x=$1
    echo $x ${x} "$x" "${x}"
    for item in $list; do
        echo $item
    done
    if [ $x = "hello" ]; then
        echo `date`
    fi
}
test_func $foo
""",
    """
foo=$bar
export A=$B
local C=$D
case $x in
    a) echo $y;;
    b) echo $z;;
esac
echo $(cat < $file)
cat <<EOF
$foo
EOF
""",
    """
echo $10
""",
    """
echo 'unclosed quote
"""
]

total = 0
passed = 0

for i, script in enumerate(complex_scripts):
    for mode in ["--syntax", "--suggest", "--syntax-suggest", "--transform", "--check"]:
        total += 1
        res1 = subprocess.run([orig_bin, mode, ""], input=script, text=True, capture_output=True)
        res2 = subprocess.run([my_bin, mode, ""], input=script, text=True, capture_output=True)

        ok = (res1.returncode == res2.returncode and res1.stdout == res2.stdout and res1.stderr == res2.stderr)
        if ok:
            passed += 1
        else:
            print(f"FAILED for script {i}, mode={mode}")
            print(f"  ORIG exit={res1.returncode}, out={res1.stdout!r}, err={res1.stderr!r}")
            print(f"  MINE exit={res2.returncode}, out={res2.stdout!r}, err={res2.stderr!r}")

# 2. File testing and --replace
with open("test_file_a.sh", "w") as f:
    f.write("echo $foo\n")
with open("test_file_b.sh", "w") as f:
    f.write("echo \"$foo\"\n")

# Test --replace on test_file_a.sh
total += 1
subprocess.run([orig_bin, "--replace", "test_file_a.sh"])
orig_content = open("test_file_a.sh").read()

with open("test_file_a.sh", "w") as f:
    f.write("echo $foo\n")
subprocess.run([my_bin, "--replace", "test_file_a.sh"])
my_content = open("test_file_a.sh").read()

if orig_content == my_content:
    passed += 1
else:
    print(f"FAILED --replace: orig={orig_content!r}, mine={my_content!r}")

os.remove("test_file_a.sh")
os.remove("test_file_b.sh")

# 3. CLI flag error testing
for flag in ["--invalid-flag", "-v", "-z"]:
    total += 1
    res1 = subprocess.run([orig_bin, flag], capture_output=True, text=True)
    res2 = subprocess.run([my_bin, flag], capture_output=True, text=True)
    if res1.returncode == res2.returncode and res1.stderr == res2.stderr:
        passed += 1
    else:
        print(f"FAILED CLI flag {flag}")
        print(f"  ORIG exit={res1.returncode}, err={res1.stderr!r}")
        print(f"  MINE exit={res2.returncode}, err={res2.stderr!r}")

# 4. Help and Version
for flag in ["-h", "--help", "--version"]:
    total += 1
    res1 = subprocess.run([orig_bin, flag], capture_output=True, text=True)
    res2 = subprocess.run([my_bin, flag], capture_output=True, text=True)
    if res1.returncode == res2.returncode and res1.stdout == res2.stdout:
        passed += 1
    else:
        print(f"FAILED flag {flag}")
        print(f"  ORIG out={res1.stdout!r}")
        print(f"  MINE out={res2.stdout!r}")

print(f"TOTAL PASSED: {passed} / {total}")
'"}

Shellharden: The corrective bash syntax highlighter.

Usage:
	shellharden [options] [files]
	cat files | shellharden [options] ''

Shellharden is a syntax highlighter and a tool to semi-automate the rewriting
of scripts to ShellCheck conformance, mainly focused on quoting.

The default mode of operation is like `cat`, but with syntax highlighting in
foreground colors and suggestive changes in background colors.

Options:
	--suggest         Output a colored diff suggesting changes.
	--syntax          Output syntax highlighting with ANSI colors.
	--syntax-suggest  Diff with syntax highlighting (default mode).
	--transform       Output suggested changes.
	--check           No output; exit with 2 if changes are suggested.
	--replace         Replace file contents with suggested changes.
	--                Don't treat further arguments as options.
	-h|--help         Show help text.
	--version         Show version.

The changes suggested by Shellharden inhibits word splitting and indirect
pathname expansion. This will make your script ShellCheck compliant in terms of
quoting. Whether your script will work afterwards is a different question:
If your script was using those features on purpose, it obviously won't anymore!

Every script is possible to write without using word splitting or indirect
pathname expansion, but it may involve doing things differently.
See the accompanying file how_to_do_things_safely_in_bash.md or online:
https://github.com/anordal/shellharden/blob/master/how_to_do_things_safely_in_bash.md
